note: Signature chart per position, per §5.2, plus the two fields the index cards read. `evaluated_on` names the family of statistics a position is judged on rather than one chart's axes — the built pages carry four to nine blocks each, so a single chart title misdescribed them. `summary` is written for the card at card length, rather than the index clamping `methodology` mid-sentence. WR and TE differ from the brief: both originally keyed on route participation, which needs a routes-run denominator no open source publishes; TE now publishes it by the operator's decision (docs/STATE.md) and WR uses target share against air yards share.

data.evaluated_on: Rushing volume, scrambles and dropback efficiency
data.summary: The passing numbers that describe a good quarterback barely move fantasy scoring. A carry is worth several times a pass attempt, and the count of runs matters where the rate does not.
data.chart_title: Rush attempts against fantasy points per game
data.caption: Carries, not completions, are what separate the top of the position.
data.methodology: Quarterback is the position where the fantasy answer and the football answer come apart hardest. The passing numbers that describe a good quarterback — accuracy over expected, time to throw — barely move fantasy scoring, while a carry is worth several times a pass attempt. What follows takes that in four steps: what rushing is actually worth, why the count of runs matters and the rate does not, where efficiency and scoring part company, and how little a pass-happy offense tells you. It is one season, so it is evidence rather than a law, and the page says where the source needed correcting.

data.evaluated_on: Opportunity, touch value and expected points
data.summary: A target is worth roughly twice a carry in PPR, and a carry inside the 10 several more. Weighting the touches that decide the position survives noise that raw counts do not.
data.caption: Backs above the line are earning more high-value work than their overall usage implies.
data.methodology: Running back scoring follows opportunity, and not all opportunity is equal. A target is worth roughly twice a carry in PPR, and a carry inside the 10 is worth several. HVT/G weights the touches that actually decide the position, and it survives the week-to-week noise that raw carry counts do not.

data.evaluated_on: Target share, air yards share and role
data.summary: A possession receiver and a vertical threat can share a WOPR and cannot share a projection. Splitting the composite shows which of the two you are actually buying.
data.chart_title: Target share against air yards share
data.caption: The two components of WOPR, plotted separately. The same composite score describes very different roles.
data.methodology: WOPR is usually quoted as a single number, which hides the thing worth knowing. A possession receiver and a vertical threat can share a WOPR and cannot share a projection. Splitting it into target share and air yards share shows which one you are buying. This replaces the brief's TPRR-based trapezoid, which needs a routes-run denominator no open source publishes.

data.evaluated_on: Route participation, target rate and yards per route
data.summary: A tight end can run almost every route his offense runs and still finish outside the top twelve. Running the route and being thrown the ball are two different jobs.
data.caption: Running the routes buys the chance; target share is whether it converts.
data.methodology: Tight end is the position where volume and role come apart. A tight end can run almost every route his offense runs and still finish outside the top twelve, because running the route and being thrown the ball are two different jobs. What follows holds role against production one pair at a time — participation against target share, then against target rate, then yardage against touchdowns, then downfield role, and finally the efficiency pair the history turns on. Every number is last season's, because a projection is an opinion and these are what an opinion has to survive.

data.summary: Turnovers and touchdowns decide the scoring and barely repeat year to year. Per-play quality is the part that carries, so it is the part worth streaming on.
data.caption: Pressure repeats week to week. Turnovers largely do not.
data.methodology: Defensive scoring is dominated by turnovers and touchdowns, both of which are close to random year over year. Pressure rate is the stable input, so it is the one worth streaming on.

data.evaluated_on: Attempt volume, distance bands and scoring environment
data.summary: Kicker scoring needs an offense good enough to reach field goal range and inefficient enough to stop there. Distance bands matter more than raw attempts.
data.chart_title: Attempts by distance band against scoring environment
data.caption: Kickers on good offences that stall inside the 35 are the ones worth having.
data.methodology: Kicker scoring needs an offence good enough to reach field goal range and inefficient enough to stop there. Distance bands matter more than raw attempts once the long-range rules are accounted for.
